transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-30
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Daniel Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Laura Chen (CTO, Suncrest), Eric Alvarez (Platform Eng), Nina Patel (Head of Security), Samir Rao (ML Eng)

---
[00:00] Daniel Park: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intro, I'm Daniel, I'm the AE on this account, Maya is our solutions engineer, she'll run through the integration options and answer technical Qs. Laura: would you like to kick off with your goals?

[00:22] Laura Chen: Sure, yeah. Thanks, Daniel. High level — Suncrest is looking to add conversational assistants across customer support and internal knowledge. We're evaluating options for running inference: we want to understand Redwood hosted, dedicated capacity, and a private VPC/on-prem route. Key constraints are data residency, control over keys, and predictable latency during market hours.

[00:40] Maya Singh: Great, that makes sense. Just to set expectations: we support a unified API across hosted, dedicated and private deployments. The integration patterns we usually see are either direct SDK calls to Redwood's hosted API, a gateway/proxy layer inside customer infra, or an SDK sidecar next to application services. Each has tradeoffs.

[01:05] Eric Alvarez: When you say gateway/proxy, are you talking about a Redwood-managed proxy or something we run? Our security team prefers to own the network path.

[01:18] Maya Singh: Good Q. We have both options. For hosted, customers often put a proxy inside their VPC that forwards to Redwood for additional controls. For Private, we can deploy the control plane endpoints into your VPC so traffic never leaves. For Dedicated, you get reserved GPU pools in our infra but you can also front it with your own gateway.

[01:40] Nina Patel: From Security perspective: we need KMS/HSM integration, audit logs retention for 7 years, SSO (SAML) + RBAC, and proof of SOC2/ISO certifications. Also want to know about data at rest encryption for embeddings and whether we can disable model logging.

[02:05] Maya Singh: On KMS we integrate with major cloud KMS and can support customer-managed keys. Audit logs are available via the Console and can be exported to your SIEM. We have an enterprise package that extends retention and audit detail. And yes, model op logs can be redaction or disabled; we support options to not persist prompts if you choose.

[02:30] Daniel Park: Quick commercial note — Dedicated gives you predictable throughput and a monthly commitment, while hosted is usage-based and faster to get started. Private/VPC gives you the maximum controls you described but requires longer lead time for deployment.

[02:50] Samir Rao: On the integration side for our engineers: we use LangChain in the retrieval pipeline and are experimenting with LlamaIndex for document stores. How smooth is the integration with your SDKs?

[03:05] Maya Singh: We provide first-class SDKs in Python/Node and example connectors for LangChain and LlamaIndex. Typical pattern is: you run an embedding pipeline (either on your side or with our embedding endpoint), store vectors, then use the retriever to construct prompts. We also include a small adapter that maps LlamaIndex retrievers to our streaming generation calls.

[03:28] Eric Alvarez: Does the wrapper support streaming tokens to the client? Our UX requires progressive token streaming for chat.

[03:36] Maya Singh: Yes — streaming is supported in hosted and dedicated, and we can enable streaming in private deployments but that depends on network/topology. One caveat: streaming performance ties into your gateway if you front with one — we recommend long-lived connections and keepalives.

[03:56] Laura Chen: About rate limits — we anticipate bursts at market open, maybe 5-10x baseline for a few minutes. Can Redwood handle burst capacity and how are quotas defined?

[04:12] Maya Singh: We have per-route and per-API-key quotas, plus burst capacity. For hosted customers we enforce token-per-minute quotas and concurrent request limits; you can request a burst window or set up dedicated capacity which gives you more predictable headroom. For Dedicated, you configure concurrency and we'll reserve GPUs; Dedicated also supports a burst pool if arranged.

[04:35] Samir Rao: Is throttling enforced at a token level or request level? We do a lot of short context, high-frequency calls.

[04:44] Maya Singh: Both. There are token-based rate limits and a request concurrency cap. For short, high-frequency calls you'd want to batch or use a prefix cache. We can suggest batching configuration and tradeoffs in the Optimize module.

[05:03] Eric Alvarez: You mentioned prefix cache — can you explain KV cache or prefix caching behavior? We've seen different latencies with long context windows.

[05:12] Maya Singh: Sure. Our runtime manages KV cache for autoregressive decoding. For repeat prefixes we can use prefix caching so the runtime doesn't recompute early layers. That reduces token cost and latency when the start of the prompt is repetitive, typical in chat apps. Works best when you have a stable system prompt and the dynamic portion is short.

[05:35] Nina Patel: On observability — we need traces aligned with our requestIds, token-level cost breakdowns per request, and Prometheus/OpenTelemetry endpoints. Does Redwood hook into our tracing?

[05:47] Maya Singh: Yes. We emit per-request traces and metrics; you can attach your trace id header and it will be part of the trace. We export Prometheus metrics and have OpenTelemetry collector compatibility. The Console surfaces token-level cost and per-route latency breakdowns.

[06:05] Laura Chen: About data residency — some data cannot leave our VPC. If we go hosted, is there a way to have embeddings or PII kept on-prem?

[06:18] Maya Singh: Two approaches: you can do embeddings on-prem and store vectors in your managed vector DB while still using hosted generation calls — retriever will assemble context locally. Or we do a Private deployment where the inference runtime is in your VPC/on-prem. Hosted doesn't meet strict data residency unless you use the hybrid approach.

[06:42] Samir Rao: For the LangChain pipeline, is there an example where retrieval and reranking happen client-side and only the final prompt hits Redwood? That would help with PII.

[06:53] Maya Singh: Absolutely. We have examples where you run candidate generation and rerankers locally, and only pass a final trimmed prompt to the model. That reduces token exposure and cost. We'll share the sample in the repo.

[07:05] Daniel Park: Quick commercial question — any regulatory verticals you need to support? Payments? Banking?

[07:12] Laura Chen: We're in regulated finance. We need auditability and the ability to demonstrate logical separation in case of audit. We also have a timeline: pilot in 6 weeks, production in ~4 months if POC looks good.

[07:25] Maya Singh: Pilot in 6 weeks is doable with hosted plus a proxy and then switch to Dedicated/Private as needed. For production in 4 months, Dedicated or Private is common. Private deployments have a longer lead time — provisioning and network setup can take a few weeks, but we accelerate those for enterprise customers.

[07:45] Nina Patel: On encryption — can you confirm customer-managed keys for both embeddings and logs? And HSM support?

[07:54] Maya Singh: Yes for Dedicated and Private we support CMKs and HSM integrations. For hosted we support CMKs in certain regions — we'll provide the exact matrix in the security deep-dive docs.

[08:08] Eric Alvarez: What about model rollouts and fallbacks? If we pin a model and it's unhealthy, do you have automatic fallback to another variant?

[08:17] Maya Singh: Yes we have rollout policies: canary, A/B, automatic fallback. Smart routing can fall back to compatible variants or lower-cost models if capacity issues occur. You can control fallback policy per-route.

[08:31] Samir Rao: Any latency guarantees or SLOs we can expect for Dedicated?

[08:38] Daniel Park: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets. We'll package SLOs in the contract. Hosted doesn't have the same strict latency SLOs but we publish performance profiles.

[08:50] Laura Chen: Observability question again — do you provide raw token traces or just aggregates? We need to debug hallucinations and see token probabilities ideally.

[08:59] Maya Singh: We provide token-level timing and cost breakdowns and sampling of model outputs for debugging, but we generally don't expose raw log probabilities for all customers. We can consider extended telemetry in enterprise plans.

[09:16] Nina Patel: For the security deep-dive, we'll need: SOC2 report, network architecture for private deployments, KMS integration docs, and sample audit logs. Also an NDA for some artifacts.

[09:26] Daniel Park: Noted. We'll share SOC2 and technical docs, and we can sign an NDA.

[09:32] Laura Chen: On quotas again — if we do a hybrid approach with embedding on-prem and hosted generation, how do you handle auth and token exchange?

[09:44] Maya Singh: We support token exchange patterns and short-lived credentials for the proxy. You can use signed JWTs from your identity provider to authenticate to Redwood through the proxy. We'll include sample exchange flows in the integration guide.

[09:58] Samir Rao: For LlamaIndex, any specific plugin or adapter? We faced schema mismatch in earlier experiments.

[10:07] Maya Singh: We maintain a lightweight adapter that normalizes LlamaIndex output into our prompt schema; it handles chunking and metadata. We'll provide sample config for retriever scoring thresholds and an example for streaming results into a chat UI.

[10:26] Eric Alvarez: Do you have limits on model context window sizes for hosted vs dedicated? We plan to use 32k for some workflows.

[10:35] Maya Singh: Supported context window depends on model family. For large context (32k) you'd typically use models we've validated on dedicated hosts; hosted has models that support large contexts but we can confirm specific model variants and their performance numbers. We'll include a performance matrix.

[10:52] Laura Chen: Can you talk about costs around embeddings + storage + generation? We're trying to estimate unit economics for the pilot.

[10:59] Daniel Park: Roughly: embeddings priced per vector, generation per token. Dedicated can lower per-token cost via reserved capacity and batching. Optimize module suggests batching, prefix caching, and quantization to reduce cost. We'll send a model-by-model cost scenario for your expected volumes.

[11:20] Nina Patel: A couple of smaller operational Qs: can we set per-team quotas and alerts? And integrate with PagerDuty?

[11:29] Maya Singh: Yes — per-key and per-route quotas, alerting, and webhook/pagerduty integration are supported. You can also surface cost anomalies via the Console.

[11:42] Samir Rao: For the POC, what's a minimal integration we can do to validate latency and cost?

[11:50] Maya Singh: I'd recommend: 1) Use hosted with a small proxy in your VPC to preserve requestIds and SSO, 2) run embeddings locally and store vectors in your DB, 3) use our SDK with LangChain retriever for 1:1 rerank and pass a trimmed prompt to Redwood; measure latency and cost. If that looks good, we can spin up Dedicated for production tests. We'll supply a step-by-step repo.

[12:14] Laura Chen: That sounds fine. Timeline: Daniel, you'll send pricing; Maya you'll send integration repo; Nina will give security questions; then schedule the security deep-dive.

[12:25] Daniel Park: Correct. Anything else?

[12:28] Eric Alvarez: One more — is there a sandbox or synthetic benchmark we can run within our environment? We want deterministic load for market open simulation.

[12:38] Maya Singh: Yes, we'll provision a trial API key and a benchmark harness that simulates token and concurrency patterns. We'll also provide guidance on harnessing the Console metrics.

[12:50] Laura Chen: Great. Thanks everyone.

[12:55] Daniel Park: Recap of next steps and owners: pricing (Daniel), integration examples (Maya), security Qs (Nina to Redwood), schedule security deep-dive. We'll follow up with calendar invites.

[13:08] Nina Patel: Thanks, bye.
